clinicalPearls: A psoriasiform, violaceous, acral dermatosis symmetrically affecting the ears, nose, fingers, toes and nails, often with adherent scale.

Almost invariably paraneoplastic and strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the upper aerodigestive tract (oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, lung) and with metastatic cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
It predominantly affects men over 40, frequently with a history of smoking and/or alcohol use.
The eruption evolves in stages: initially acral (ears, nose, digits, nails) while the tumour is occult, then extending to the hands, feet and cheeks, and eventually more widely as disease advances.
Nail dystrophy, paronychia-like change and a painful palmoplantar keratoderma are common features.
Skin disease is typically resistant to topical therapy but improves with treatment of the underlying carcinoma, and recurrence signals tumour relapse.
It must be distinguished from the unrelated Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome, an inherited disorder featuring follicular atrophoderma and early basal cell carcinomas.
reference.pathophysiology: The pathogenesis of acrokeratosis paraneoplastica is uncertain. Proposed mechanisms include tumour-derived growth factors such as transforming growth factor alpha, insulin-like growth factor 1 and epidermal growth factor driving epidermal hyperproliferation. An immunological hypothesis invokes molecular mimicry, whereby antibodies or cytotoxic T cells directed against tumour antigens cross-react with structurally similar antigens in the epidermis and basement membrane zone. Disturbances of zinc and vitamin A metabolism have also been implicated. The acral distribution and the close temporal relationship with tumour activity favour a humoral, tumour-related process.
additionalDifferentials: Psoriasis, especially acral or palmoplantar disease
Chronic acral eczema or hyperkeratotic hand and foot dermatitis
Systemic or chilblain lupus erythematosus with acral involvement
Dermatophyte (tinea) infection of the hands and feet
additionalInvestigations: ENT examination with nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for upper aerodigestive squamous carcinoma
CT or MRI of the head and neck, chest and mediastinum
Panendoscopy including oesophagoscopy and bronchoscopy as indicated
Biopsy of cervical lymphadenopathy for metastatic squamous carcinoma
Skin biopsy showing non-specific hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis and dyskeratosis
PET-CT to locate an occult primary when initial imaging is negative
redFlags: Acral psoriasiform eruption in a middle-aged male smoker or drinker
Nail dystrophy with violaceous acral scaling unresponsive to topical therapy
Cervical lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, hoarseness or haemoptysis
Recurrence of the eruption after tumour treatment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis reflects the associated squamous cell carcinoma, which is often advanced with regional nodal spread at diagnosis; the skin lesions typically resolve with successful tumour therapy and their recurrence heralds relapse.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the eruption as treatment-resistant psoriasis or eczema and delaying the tumour search
Confusing it with the unrelated Bazex-Dupre-Christol genodermatosis
Not performing ENT and aerodigestive evaluation when the primary is occult
Overlooking recurrence as a marker of tumour relapse
